questions.enonce_markdown:
Using specific examples explain the following forms of nutrition.

(i) Mutualism.

(ii) Saprophytic nutrition. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Mutualism** *(3 marks)*

**Mutualism** is a close association between organisms of **two different species in which both partners benefit**. Examples:

- **Rhizobium and leguminous plants** (bean, groundnut): the bacteria live in **root nodules** and **fix atmospheric nitrogen** into ammonia/nitrogen compounds used by the plant; the bacteria receive **carbohydrates** and a protected habitat from the plant.
- **Lichens**: an **alga (or cyanobacterium)** photosynthesises and supplies **sugars**, while the **fungus** supplies **water, mineral ions, attachment and protection from drying**.
- **Cellulose-digesting bacteria and protozoa in the rumen of cattle**: the microbes digest cellulose, which the host cannot do, and the host receives fatty acids (and the microbes as protein); the microbes receive food and a warm, anaerobic habitat.

**(ii) Saprophytic nutrition** *(4 marks)*

In **saprophytic nutrition** an organism (a **saprophyte**) feeds on **dead and decaying organic matter** (dead plants, animals, faeces). It is a form of **heterotrophic nutrition** with **extracellular digestion**:

1. The saprophyte **secretes digestive enzymes** (amylase, proteases, lipases) **onto the dead material**.
2. The large insoluble molecules are broken down **outside the body** into soluble molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids).
3. The soluble products are **absorbed** into the cells through the cell surface (by diffusion and active transport) and used for respiration and growth.

*Example: Rhizopus (bread mould, or Mucor).* The **hyphae** grow over and into the bread; **rhizoids** secrete enzymes and absorb the digested food; the large branching **mycelium** gives a very large absorbing surface. Other examples are mushrooms, yeast and many soil bacteria. Saprophytes are the **decomposers** that recycle nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals) in ecosystems.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Describe how the alimentary canal of a named herbivore is adapted to its diet.

(ii) What are the functions of the stomach in mammals? *[13 marks]* *(3, 4, 8, 5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The cow (a ruminant herbivore)** *(8 marks)*

The diet (grass) is **rich in cellulose, bulky and low in protein**, and mammals produce **no cellulase**. The alimentary canal is adapted in these ways:

| Part | Adaptation |
|---|---|
| **Teeth** | **Incisors** only in the lower jaw; the upper jaw has a hard **dental pad** against which the incisors cut grass. A gap (**diastema**) replaces the canines. **Premolars and molars** are broad with **ridges of enamel** and the lower jaw moves sideways to **grind** the grass finely, which breaks cell walls and gives a large surface for enzymes and microbes. |
| **Salivary glands** | Large glands produce a lot of **alkaline saliva** (hydrogencarbonate), which lubricates the food and **buffers the rumen pH**. |
| **Stomach in 4 chambers** | **Rumen**: a very large fermentation chamber where **symbiotic bacteria and protozoa secrete cellulase** and digest cellulose to **fatty acids**, which are absorbed through the rumen wall; the microbes also make amino acids and **vitamin B**. **Reticulum**: honeycomb walls; forms the food into small balls (**cud**) that are **regurgitated** and chewed again (rumination). **Omasum**: many folds; **absorbs water** from the food. **Abomasum**: the true (glandular) stomach, secretes **HCl and pepsin**, which digest protein, including the dead microbes. |
| **Small intestine** | **Very long** (about 40 m in a cow) with villi, giving **time and surface area** for the digestion and absorption of the poorly digestible food. |
| **Caecum and colon** | The caecum is small in ruminants (it is large in non-ruminants such as the rabbit, where it is the fermentation chamber). The **long colon** reabsorbs water and mineral ions before the faeces are egested. |

**(ii) Functions of the stomach in mammals** *(5 marks)*

1. **Temporary storage** of food, so the animal can eat a large meal and food enters the intestine slowly and in small amounts.
2. **Churning**: muscular contractions (peristalsis) of the wall **mix the food with gastric juice** to form **chyme**.
3. **Secretion of hydrochloric acid** (from oxyntic cells): it gives pH 1.5 to 2 so that **pepsin works at its optimum**, **converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin**, **kills most bacteria** swallowed with the food and softens the food.
4. **Chemical digestion of proteins**: **pepsin** hydrolyses proteins to polypeptides; in young mammals **rennin** clots milk protein (casein) so it stays longer in the stomach.
5. **Mucus** secreted by goblet cells **protects the stomach wall** from acid and enzymes and lubricates the food.
6. Secretion of **intrinsic factor**, needed to absorb **vitamin B12**; release of the hormone **gastrin**, which stimulates the gastric glands.
7. **Regulated release** of chyme into the duodenum through the **pyloric sphincter**; a small amount of **absorption** (water, alcohol, some drugs).
